pages.text: NASA's Gateways to Blue Skies (GBS) Competition | USAGov Skip to main content NASA's Gateways to Blue Skies (GBS) Competition Submit ideas to improve the reliability and efficiency of NASA's infrastructure. NASA's 2027 GBS Competition asks teams of two to six (2-6) college students to conceptualize innovative airborne platforms for inspecting land-based infrastructure. The goal is to implement the solution by 2035 to improve safety, reliability, efficiency, and cost. Based on reviews of proposals and 2-minute video submissions, up to 8 finalist teams will be selected to receive $9,000 and advance to Phase 2. In the second phase, the finalists will present at a forum in May 2027. Eligible winners will receive NASA internships. pages.text: NASA's Human Lander Challenge (HuLC) | USAGov Skip to main content NASA's Human Lander Challenge (HuLC) Develop a system to enable communications for lunar landers NASA's Human Lander Challenge (HuLC) invites collegiate teams to develop innovative systems-level solutions to understand, establish, and optimize lunar communications systems. The systems will be for landers and surface level operations and will be implemented in 3 to 5 years. Each team will submit a proposal and a two minute video. Twelve finalist teams will receive $9,000 and advance to Phase 2. In Phase 2, finalists will present at a forum in Huntsville, AL in June 2027. The top three teams will share an $18,000 prize. pages.title: NASA: Ocean Worlds
pages.text: NASA: Ocean Worlds Next What is the ultimate origin of water? A water molecule is made up of one oxygen and two hydrogen atoms. Hydrogen was created in the Big Bang and oxygen in the cores of stars more massive than the Sun. Enormous amounts of water, in gaseous form, exist in the vast stellar nurseries of our galaxy. The Hubble Space Telescope peered into the Helix Nebula and found water molecules. Hydrogen and oxygen, formed by different processes, combine to make water molecules in the ejected atmosphere of this dying star. The origins of our oceans are in the stars. Next Water molecules exist in the Orion Nebula and are still forming today. The nebula is composed mostly of hydrogen gas; other molecules are comparatively rare. Even so, the nebula is so vast that it creates enough water every day to fill Earth’s oceans 60 times over. Water, along with every other molecule created in these stellar nurseries, becomes raw material for the formation of new planetary systems. Next Water molecules are abundant in planetary systems forming around other stars. Water molecules have been found around the 20-million-year-old star Beta Pictoris, where a huge disk of dust and gas hints at collisions between comets, asteroids, and young planets (artist’s conception). Next Asteroids and comets are debris left over from the formation of our solar system and are rich in water. These small bodies are time capsules that contain tantalizing clues about what our solar system was like 4.5 billion years ago. pages.text: Nat Geo's Ultimate Guide to Birding in Los Angeles | National Geographic ANIMALS Nat Geo's Guide to Birding in La La Land Birds like the warm weather in Los Angeles just as much as humans. Author and birding expert Noah Strycker shares the best places to spot everything from warblers to jays. The sprawling city's parks, ecological reserves, and shores offer ample opportunity for celebrity bird sightings. David Billet By Noah Strycker Published October 2, 2026 Whether you’re new in town or a lifelong Angeleno, Los Angeles holds a delightful secret: It hosts one of the hottest birding scenes north of the Mexican border. Amid the Hollywood glamour and urban sprawl, the City of Angels boasts a surprisingly rich variety of birdlife. More wild bird species have been spotted in Los Angeles County—561, according to the most recent count from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s eBird database —than any other county within the United States and Canada. Extending from turquoise beaches on the west side to the rugged San Gabriel Mountains surrounding the eastern skyline, the U.S.’s second-largest metropolitan area attracts flying creatures for the same reasons people flock to it—warm weather year round, tasty food, chances to mate, and nice housing. The joy of L.A. birding has been an open secret among dedicated locals for decades, but lately, word has spread. Bird watching soared during the COVID-19 pandemic years, when cooped-up urbanites fled to the great outdoors en masse . El Bulevar del Paso Natchez con sus 444 millas (715 km) conmemora un antiguo sendero (el "Old Trace" [Viejo paso]) que conectaba partes del sur del río Misisipi, pasando por Alabama, hasta los depósitos naturales de sal en la parte central actual de Tennessee. Hoy en día el público puede disfrutar la Carretera Escénica Nacional/Ruta Americana manejando, caminando, andando en bicicleta, montando a caballo o acampando. Algunos tramos del sendero Old Trace nos conectan con la historia de los pueblos a través de los siglos. Los viajeros más homenajeados del Paso Natchez fueron los granjeros y navegantes de las regiones del río Ohio en Pensilvania, Ohio y Kentucky, junto con los suministros producto de la pesca con caña de Kentucky enviados a los puertos de Natchez y Nueva Orleans a comienzos de la década de 1800. Music Nate Chinen's Top 10 Albums of 2025 December 11, 2025 5:00 AM ET Nate Chinen My No. 1 album of 2025: Mary Halvorson's About Ghosts It usually only takes an instant to recognize the sound Mary Halvorson gets out of her hollow-body guitar: percussive but pliable, with the odd subversive wobble. Her voice as a composer and orchestrator is no less unmistakable, as she proves on About Ghosts , a thinking person's thrill ride that supplements her hyperacute chamber-jazz ensemble, Amaryllis, with a pair of terrific saxophonists, Brian Settles and Immanuel Wilkins. The guests make their presence known, joining a dynamic roster of improvisers that also includes trumpeter Adam O'Farrill, trombonist Jacob Garchik and vibraphonist Patricia Brennan (each of whom dropped their own worthy albums this year). Listen carefully and you'll hear traces of the "Pocket Piano" synthesizer that sparked Halvorson's creativity as a composer, along with a heartfelt tribute to a former bandmate, the pedal steel guitar genius Susan Alcorn, who died early this year. Modern jazz is forever evolving — and so are those in active dialogue with that tradition, as Halvorson and her intrepid colleagues keep reminding us. pages.text: Nathaniel Philbrick's New Book Could Give You Whiplash | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE Nathaniel Philbrick's New Book Could Give You Whiplash The best-selling historian sits down with National Geographic to talk about his fast-paced new book that places San Francisco at the center of American events. A miner's camp on the hillside in El Dorado, California during the gold rush. The history-making event is the subject of a new book by Nathaniel Philbrick. Library of Congress By William O'Connor Published October 6, 2026 However chaotic life may seem, cracking open the latest book from historian Nathaniel Philbrick will make it calm by comparison. The author behind the best-selling In the Heart of the Sea is out with a new work, The Rush: California Gold, the Civil War, and the Making of the Modern World , which chronicles the mad dash to San Francisco in 1849 after gold was accidentally discovered there. The book is action-packed, with page after page of gun-toting politicians, treasonous plots, and unspeakable misery heaped on humans by other humans. Philbrick takes a tale we all think we know enough about— the 49ers —and unravels that tight little story into a series of characters and vignettes that leave one slack-jawed at the topsy-turvy era. All of the tales in the book are in service of a very ambitious goal Philbrick lays out in the title—rethinking the gold rush as more than a merely curious event in American history and instead as one that transformed the country and sent it hurtling toward its fate—the coming civil war. DWGs provide supplemental funding in response to major economic dislocations or other events that cause or contribute to a shortage of existing WIOA Dislocated Worker formula funds and other relevant resources in states and local areas, creating challenges in their ability to provide workforce services to eligible participants. DWGs enable states and communities to respond to and recover from large, often unexpected dislocation events and their associated impacts. The WIOA statute allows the Employment and Training Administration (ETA) to fund two types of DWGs: Disaster Recovery and Employment Recovery. pages.text: National Experimental Well-Being Statistics (NEWS) National Experimental Well-Being Statistics (NEWS) Skip Navigation National Experimental Well-Being Statistics (NEWS) July 14, 2025 This is the third release of the NEWS project, covering 2016 to 2021. The NEWS project aims to produce the best possible estimates of income and poverty given all available survey, decennial census, administrative, and third-party data. We estimate improved income and poverty statistics by addressing bias from unit non-response, missing information, and measurement error. Relative to the previous version , this release Adds five additional years of income and poverty estimates, Allows comparisons of income and poverty estimates over time by demographic subgroup, and Uses administrative data to better model tax credits during the Pandemic, such as Economic Impact Payments. Scientists and engineers from industry, academia, and government agencies can collaborate with NIST researchers to address critical technical problems that promote U.S. innovation and industrial competitiveness by advancing measurement science, standards, and technology for engineered systems in ways to enhance economic security and improve quality of life. Research areas include: Advancement of real-scale structural-fire measurements, Generation of technical data to improve fire & building codes, Validation of physics-based models, and Post-fire investigations. Photo by NPS. The National Park Service and the American Geosciences Institute host the annual National Fossil Day celebration during Earth Science Week in October. National Fossil Day is a celebration organized to promote public awareness and stewardship of fossils, as well as to foster a greater appreciation of their scientific and educational value. Fossils discovered on the nation's public lands preserve ancient life from all major eras of Earth's history, and from every major group of animal or plant. In the national parks, for example, fossils range from primitive algae found high in the mountains of Glacier National Park, Montana, to the remains of ice-age animals found in caves at Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona.
